title: regional-failover-execution-retrospective-q1-2025
body:
Executive summary:

This doc is a working retrospective of the partial regional outage that occurred on 2025-03-14 03:42 UTC affecting the eu-west-1 region and causing elevated latency and 502 spikes for hosted-api endpoints pinned to eu-west-1. Traffic was shifted to warm-standby (eu-central-1) using our emergency routing policy and DNS TTL override. Total customer impact window ~22 minutes for some routes; larger customers observed degraded p95 for ~45 minutes due to downstream retries.

High-level impact:
- A subset of inference endpoints (hosted-api model routing tier) saw 40-70% request errors (502/503) and worker queue growth.
- Autoscaling in eu-west-1 did not relieve queueing due to container eviction race with autoscaler leader election.
- Warm-standby (eu-central-1) had capacity headroom but default routing weights and DNS TTLs delayed failover by ~7 minutes.

What we ran: sequence of actions (play-by-play)
- 03:42: alert triggered: api-error-rate-eu-west1 > 20% for 2m (pager to oncall)
- 03:43: oncall ack, pulled dashboards (trace, queue length, instance metrics). Noted worker pod restarts and node evictions.
- 03:45: SRE lead requested temporary increase of routing weight for eu-central-1 via SmartRouter console (manual route override).
- 03:48: initial routing weight change applied; however DNS still pointed many clients to eu-west-1 due to 60s TTL + intermediate caches.
- 03:50: executed DNS emergency TTL override to 5s for hostnames used by platform gateway (internal/external). Change propagated by 03:56 to most resolvers.
- 03:56: traffic shift finished; error rates returned to baseline by 04:04.
- 04:10: began controlled rollback and runbook review while monitoring for reoccurrence.

Detection and monitoring notes:
- First signal came from synthetic probes (internal canaries) and error budgets rather than customer reports. Probing cadence was 30s; ideal would be 15s for critical routes.
- Alerts were noisy at first: multiple derived alerts for 50x errors in different aggregations. Need single synthesis alert in pager for regional service-level outage.

Runbook steps executed (condensed):
1) Confirm scope: check model routing table, node pools, autoscaler events.
2) Attempt local remediation (drain + restart pods) - not effective due to eviction timing.
3) Increase warm-standby routing weight in SmartRouter to 90% for failing routes.
4) Lower DNS TTL for platform hostnames and then proactively clear internal resolver caches (kube-dns flush job).
5) Monitor until error rate and latency recover.

Observed deviations from runbook and why:
- Runbook assumes TTL overrides propagate in ~60s; observed real-world propagation varied 3-10 minutes depending on cloud provider and public resolvers. Need explicit note that some clients (enterprise caches, ISPs) may hold longer.
- Runbook did not include an explicit step to flush internal resolver caches; this cost us ~2 minutes. Add cross-check in playbook.
- We attempted autoscaler-driven scaling first; playbook suggests failover before expanding capacity when errors are 50%+, to avoid churn. Oncall hesitated to fail over immediately.

Root cause hypothesis (working):
Primary: A control-plane instability in eu-west-1 triggered a sequence of node evictions during a maintenance window restart of a storage component (unrelated infra) which created transient API latencies and worker restarts. Those pod restarts increased queueing in frontends which then returned 502s when request timeouts hit.
Secondary: SmartRouter routing weights and DNS TTLs were not aligned for rapid regional failover; default TTL of 60s plus public resolver behaviors slowed client migration.

Metrics snapshot (peak):
- API 5xx rate: peaked at 64% for affected endpoints (03:46 UTC)
- p95 latency for text-gen endpoints in eu-west-1: increased from 340ms to 2.1s
- Warm-standby CPU util in eu-central-1 pre-shift: 28% -> post-shift peak 65%
- Error budget burn for hosted-api global: 0.8% -> 4.9% during incident window

Notable customer effects (examples):
- Customer A (large multi-tenant SaaS) observed repeated 502s for background batch jobs; they retried and increased overall load -> our warm standby saw short surge but remained within capacity.
- Some enterprise customers with strict DNS caching policies remained routed to eu-west-1 for >8 minutes causing extended degradation. We contacted their account teams to explain impact.

Immediate remediation follow-ups (owners and dates):
- Shorten platform public TTL default from 60s -> 15s for critical hostnames (owner: Samir Patel, due: 2025-03-25)
- Update SRE runbook: add explicit resolver cache flush step and decision threshold for routing vs. scale (owner: Lina Gómez, due: 2025-03-22)
- Add synthesized regional outage alert to reduce noisy pages (owner: Ethan Park, due: 2025-03-20)
- Create post-incident test for TTL override: simulated failover drill with external resolvers (owner: Riley Morgan, due: 2025-04-01)

Longer-term action items:
- Investigate autoscaler leader election and eviction race in eu-west-1 node pool (owner: infra-team, ticket: JIRA-INFRA-1234, due: 2025-04-15)
- Add capacity buffer to warm-standby pools for high-risk time windows (owner: platform-eng, due: 2025-04-30)
- Improve SmartRouter API to support preflight failover simulations and dry-run weight changes (owner: serving-runtime, due: 2025-05-15)

Draft checklist for future regional failovers (to be incorporated into runbook):
- Confirm scope and mark impacted routes in SmartRouter.
- Check autoscaler events and node eviction logs.
- If >30% errors or sustained p95 > 2x baseline for 3min -> execute warm-standby routing weight increase to 80%.
- Immediately perform DNS TTL override to 5s for critical hostnames and run kube-dns flush job across clusters.
- Open channel to account/ops for customers with long TTLs; consider transient traffic shaping by ETag gating.
- Monitor traces for tail latency regressions; keep rollback plan ready.
- After stabilization, run controlled rollback and runbook retrospective.

Open questions / discussion items:
- What is an acceptable default TTL given tradeoffs between cache efficiency and failover time? 15s vs 30s? Need infra cost and resolver behavior analysis.
- Should failover be automated for specific health signals (queue length + 5xx) or require manual SRE approval? Risk: automation may cause oscillation during noisy signals.
- How do we better surface long-lived DNS caches from enterprise customers before incidents? Account tagging?

Appendix: quick commands used during incident (notes to self)
- SmartRouter weight change: srctl set-weight --route hosted-api-eu --region eu-central-1 --weight 0.9
- DNS TTL override: terraform apply -var="zone=platform.example.com" -target="dns_record.hosted-api.ttl_5s"
- kube-dns flush job: kubectl create job dns-flush -n kube-system --image=busybox -- /bin/sh -c "pkill -HUP -f dnsmasq"

Retrospective notes (tone: rough, action-focused):
- We successfully prevented a prolonged outage by shifting to warm-standby; however, our tooling and defaults increased mean time to recover by several minutes.
- The main human friction was uncertainty around whether to scale vs shift. Clarify decision thresholds and make them prescriptive.
- This incident is a good candidate for a full failover drill in Q2 with external resolver partners and an account-managed test with our top 5 enterprise customers.

Next steps: finalize runbook edits, schedule tabletop on 2025-03-26, and run a TTL propagation test with simulated failover on 2025-04-01.

Notes to self: convert this doc into Confluence page after PR sign-off and add timeline logs from pagerduty export (SRE-204) into ticket.
